clinicalPearls: A rare, genetically heterogeneous autosomal recessive disorder combining early-onset nephrotic syndrome with microcephaly and central nervous system anomalies.
Causative mutations affect genes encoding the KEOPS complex (including OSGEP, TP53RK, TPRKB and LAGE3) and other genes such as WDR73 involved in transfer RNA modification and cellular homeostasis.
Nephrotic syndrome is typically steroid-resistant, presenting in infancy or early childhood, and biopsy shows focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or diffuse mesangial sclerosis.
Neurological features include microcephaly (often progressive), developmental delay, seizures and gyration abnormalities on brain imaging.
Dysmorphic facial features, hiatus hernia and other extrarenal anomalies are variably present.
The combination of brain and podocyte involvement reflects shared dependence on the affected molecular pathways in both neurones and podocytes.
Phenotype and age of onset vary with the underlying gene, ranging from severe neonatal disease to milder later-onset forms.
Management is supportive, as the steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome does not respond to immunosuppression and neurological disease is progressive.
reference.pathophysiology: Galloway-Mowat syndrome is a genetically heterogeneous condition in which mutations disrupt fundamental cellular processes shared by podocytes and neurones. A major group of causative genes encodes subunits of the KEOPS complex (OSGEP, TP53RK, TPRKB and LAGE3), which is required for a universal transfer RNA modification essential for accurate messenger RNA translation; impaired function compromises protein synthesis and cellular integrity in highly specialised cells. Other implicated genes, such as WDR73, and additional loci participate in cytoskeletal regulation and cellular homeostasis. Because both the glomerular podocyte and the developing brain are exquisitely sensitive to these translational and cytoskeletal disturbances, their failure produces the characteristic dual phenotype: podocyte injury manifesting as steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and impaired neuronal proliferation and migration manifesting as microcephaly, abnormal gyration and neurodevelopmental impairment. The breadth of the phenotype, including facial dysmorphism, hiatus hernia and skeletal features, reflects the widespread requirement for these pathways during development, and the specific gene and mutation influence severity and the age at which renal and neurological disease appear.

additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing including panels for KEOPS complex genes (OSGEP, TP53RK, TPRKB, LAGE3), WDR73 and other associated loci
Renal biopsy showing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or diffuse mesangial sclerosis
Quantification of proteinuria and serum albumin
Brain imaging for microcephaly, gyration abnormalities and atrophy
Parental carrier testing and genetic counselling
redFlags: Early-onset steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with severe hypoalbuminaemia and oedema
Complications of severe nephrotic syndrome such as thrombosis or infection
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, particularly in early-onset forms, with progressive neurological deterioration and progression of nephrotic syndrome to kidney failure; many severely affected children die in infancy or early childhood. Milder, later-onset forms have a somewhat better but still guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Treating the nephrotic syndrome as steroid-sensitive and exposing the child to ineffective immunosuppression
Failing to recognise the unifying diagnosis when renal and neurological problems are assessed in isolation
Attributing microcephaly to an unrelated cause and missing the syndromic link
Not pursuing broad genetic testing given the marked genetic heterogeneity
Omitting genetic counselling for a recessive condition with recurrence risk
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics (standard reference)
management: No curative therapy exists and the steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome does not respond to immunosuppression, so management is largely supportive
Supportive management of the nephrotic syndrome with dietary sodium restriction, diuretics for oedema and consideration of renin-angiotensin system blockade to reduce proteinuria
Antiseizure medications for seizures and early-intervention developmental therapies for delay
Renal replacement therapy with dialysis and consideration of transplantation as kidney failure progresses in selected patients
Nutritional support and management of feeding difficulties, including hiatus hernia
Surveillance of renal function, proteinuria, growth, neurological status and brain imaging with serial assessment
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with molecular confirmation and family screening
Multidisciplinary and palliative care with paediatric nephrology, neurology and clinical genetics
